title: "Bias and equity: the proxy problem"
subtitle: "AIM-3 · about 90 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. State the proxy problem in one sentence, and identify the substituted
   quantity in an algorithm you have not seen before.
2. Walk the Obermeyer analysis from the choice of prediction target to the
   measured harm to the correction, including the size of the correction.
3. For a case you choose, name the proxy or data gap, the population harmed
   and the decision that went differently for them, the correction that
   followed, and that correction's adoption status today, including where the
   honest answer is "still draft" or "still contested".
4. Tell a harm of allocation from a harm of representation, and social bias
   from statistical bias.
5. Say what a clinician can and cannot catch at the bedside without seeing a
   model's internals, and cite the evidence that clinicians do not reliably
   catch a biased model even when it explains itself.
:::

**Time.** About 25 minutes of reading, 25 minutes of listening, 35 minutes of
doing, and 5 minutes to write your answer to the standing question. You need
a PubMed tab. A chatbot is optional and used for one step you can skip; your
institutional ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account is enough if you use it. Nothing
installs, and nothing here touches a patient's data.

## The number on the monitor

It is 3 a.m. on your sub-internship and you are cross-covering a medicine
floor. A nurse calls about a 61-year-old man admitted with pneumonia. He is
breathing faster than he was at midnight, he is using his neck muscles, and he
has stopped finishing his sentences. You go and look. He is a Black man with
dark skin, sweating, leaning forward on the bed. The monitor says his oxygen
saturation is 94 percent on two liters.

::: {.vendor-slide}
<div class="brand">Bed 14 · bedside monitor</div>
<h4>Vitals, 03:08</h4>
<div class="stats">
<div class="stat"><b>94%</b><span>SpO<sub>2</sub> · 2 L NC</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>28</b><span>resp / min</span></div>
<div class="stat"><b>112</b><span>pulse</span></div>
</div>
<div class="foot">Patient tripoding, accessory muscle use, speaking in three-word phrases</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative bedside display for this chapter; not a real device's screen.</div>
:::

Ninety-four is a number that lets you go back to bed. The patient in front
of you is not. You have a choice: believe the number, or believe the man.
You draw an arterial blood gas. The arterial saturation, measured directly
from his blood, comes back at 86 percent.

The pulse oximeter was not broken. It was doing what it was designed to do:
shine red and infrared light through a fingertip, measure how much of each
comes out the other side, and convert that into a saturation using a
calibration curve built from volunteers. Most of the volunteers had light
skin. Skin pigment absorbs some of the light too, and the device cannot tell
pigment from hemoglobin. For this man, at this saturation, the number on the
monitor was eight points too kind.

Nobody in the room, including the patient, knew that the device had been
calibrated on people who did not look like him. Hold that thought; the
chapter comes back to it.

## Why this matters

![The device in the opening scenario. Pulse oximeter on a patient's finger in
a hospital in Benin, 2021. Photo: Adoscam,
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) (reuse
requires the same licence), via
[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Saturom%C3%A8tre_appliqu%C3%A9_au_doigt_humain_dans_h%C3%B4pital_au_B%C3%A9nin_01.jpg).
The reading, 97 percent, is exactly the kind of number this chapter is
about.](../images/pulse-oximeter-benin.jpg){#fig-oximeter fig-alt="A fingertip pulse oximeter clipped to the index finger of a dark-skinned hand, displaying an oxygen saturation of 97 and a pulse of 92, resting on a clinic desk with paperwork behind it."}

In your first month of residency you will act on the output of at least a
dozen algorithms that nobody will describe to you as algorithms: the pulse
oximeter, the estimated kidney function on the lab report, the sepsis alert,
the risk score that decides who gets a care coordinator, the reference range
on a spirometry printout. Most of them work. Several of them are known to work
worse for some of your patients than for others, and the ones that fail do so
in the same way, for the same reason. Learning that one reason is faster than
learning the list, and it transfers to the tools that do not have a paper
written about them yet.

The second reason is about you specifically. The evidence in this chapter
says a clinician at the bedside can catch some of these failures and cannot
catch others, and that the line between them is not where most people put it.
Knowing which side of the line a tool is on tells you whether your own
vigilance is a defense or a comfort.

## The idea

### One problem, many cases

Every well-documented case of an algorithm harming patients along racial
lines in the last decade has the same shape. A quantity that mattered could
not be measured directly. Something that *could* be measured was substituted
for it. The substitution was reasonable when it was made, and it was wrong in
a way that tracked existing inequity, because the measurable thing was
measurable precisely because the health system had already been collecting
it, and the health system had already been treating people differently.

The substituted quantity is called a **proxy**: a stand-in that is measured
because the real thing cannot be. The **proxy problem** is the whole chapter
in one sentence: *an algorithm is only as fair as the relationship between
what it measures and what you hoped it measured, and that relationship can
differ by group.*

You met an instance of this in the critical appraisal chapter without the
name. There, a benchmark score in an FDA decision summary stood in for
clinical performance, and an analysis of 130 such summaries found that about
half reported any clinical performance data at all [@pmid:33820998]. The
proxy in that case was a test-set number standing in for "works on patients
like mine". This chapter is the same failure with a different quantity in the
gap.

### Case one: light standing in for oxygen

Start with the device from the opening scenario, because it is the case
where the proxy is physical and the bedside signal is real.

A pulse oximeter does not measure oxygen. It measures the ratio of red to
infrared light absorbed by a fingertip and converts that ratio into a
saturation using a curve fitted on healthy volunteers who were desaturated
under controlled conditions. The proxy is light absorbance; the quantity that
matters is arterial oxygen saturation. The two agree closely in the people the
curve was fitted on.

In December 2020, Sjoding and colleagues compared paired readings, a pulse
oximeter value and an arterial blood gas drawn within ten minutes of each
other, in two cohorts [@pmid:33326721]. They looked for **occult hypoxemia**:
an arterial saturation below 88 percent, which is treatment-changing, while
the oximeter read 92 to 96 percent, which is reassuring. In the University of
Michigan cohort it occurred in 11.7 percent of Black patients' readings and
3.6 percent of White patients'. In a multicenter cohort of 178 hospitals the
figures were 17.0 and 6.2 percent. Black patients had nearly three times the
rate of a dangerously low saturation that the device called normal.

Two larger studies confirmed the pattern and traced it forward to a decision.
Across 30,039 paired readings in Veterans Health Administration general
wards, occult hypoxemia was more likely in Black than White patients
[@pmid:35793817]. Among 1,216 patients with COVID-19 at Johns Hopkins, Fawzy
and colleagues found occult hypoxemia in 28.5 percent of Black, 29.8 percent
of Hispanic, and 30.2 percent of Asian patients, against 17.2 percent of
White patients, and then followed what happened next: Black patients had a 29
percent lower hazard, roughly a 29 percent lower rate at any given moment, of
being recognized as eligible for oxygen-threshold COVID-19 therapies, a
median delay of one hour among those eventually
recognized, and 451 patients never had their eligibility recognized at all,
most of them Black [@pmid:35639368]. That is the pathway from proxy to harm
made concrete: a number that looked fine, a treatment threshold not reached
on paper, a therapy given late or not given.

![Occult hypoxemia by race across four cohorts. Redrawn from the published
numbers in Sjoding et al. 2020 [@pmid:33326721], Valbuena et al. 2022
[@pmid:35793817], and Fawzy et al. 2022 [@pmid:35639368]. Definitions of
"normal" oximeter reading differ between studies, so compare the bars within
a cohort rather than across cohorts.](../images/occult-hypoxemia-by-race.svg){#fig-occult fig-alt="Grouped bar chart of occult hypoxemia rates in four cohorts. Michigan 2020: White 3.6 percent, Black 11.7 percent. 178 hospitals 2014 to 2015: White 6.2, Black 17.0. VA general care 2013 to 2019: White 15.6, Black 19.6, Hispanic 16.2. Johns Hopkins COVID-19: White 17.2, Black 28.5, Hispanic 29.8, Asian 30.2. In every cohort the Black bar is taller than the White bar."}

**The correction, and where it stands.** The FDA's 2013 guidance for pulse
oximeter clearance asked manufacturers to include "at least 2 darkly
pigmented subjects or 15% of your subject pool, whichever is larger" in a
study of roughly ten volunteers. In January 2025 the agency issued a draft
guidance proposing larger studies with a specified spread of skin
pigmentation, measured objectively rather than by self-report, and a label
statement on whether the device performed comparably across pigmentation
[@pmid:40042945]. The FDA's page for that guidance still carries the line
"Draft. Not for implementation. Contains non-binding recommendations."
[VERIFY: draft status checked 2026-09-07 on fda.gov; confirm before assigning]{.verify}
A 2025 preprint that tested 34 oximeters against the anticipated criteria
found that only one of the 34 passed the draft FDA standard, and that eleven
devices showed more positive bias in darkly than lightly pigmented
participants while others did not [@pmid:40832401]. The pulse oximeter on
your ward tonight is, in all likelihood, a device cleared under the 2013
rule.

This is the case with the encouraging bedside answer. A saturation that does
not match a patient's work of breathing, mentation, or color is a
discrepancy any clinician can register without knowing what
photoplethysmography, the light-measurement technique inside the device, is.
The blood gas is the check. The catch is that you have to look at the patient
rather than the number, and the number was designed to be looked at.

The sentence for a co-intern: *when the number and the patient disagree,
believe the patient and get the direct measurement.* It is also, for this
one case, the whole correction available to you tonight.

### Case two: cost standing in for need

The anchor case for this chapter is not a device. It is a risk score, and it
is the case where the bedside answer is bleak.

In 2019 Obermeyer and colleagues dissected a commercial algorithm used by
health systems across the United States to decide which patients should be
enrolled in high-risk care management programs: extra nursing contact, care
coordination, the scarce resource [@pmid:31649194]. Walk it in order, because
every step was defensible on its own.

**The job.** There are far more patients than program slots. Something has to
rank them by who would benefit most from extra care.

**The measurement problem.** "Who would benefit most from extra care" is not
a column in any database. Nobody records it; it is not even well defined
without a counterfactual, a record of what would have happened to the same
patient without the program. So the model's **prediction target**, the thing
it is trained to predict, became something that *is* in the database and
that plausibly tracks need: future health care costs. Sicker
patients cost more. Before reading on, argue for this choice. Cost is
objective, universally recorded, continuous, and available for every patient
without collecting anything new. It is exactly the choice a competent team
makes.

**The failure.** Cost measures health care *consumed*, not illness. The
health system spent less on Black patients than on White patients at the same
level of illness, because of reduced access, lower treatment intensity, and
every other documented disparity in what gets spent on whom. The algorithm
was accurate at what it predicted and systematically wrong at what it was
used for. At the 97th risk percentile, the threshold for automatic
enrollment, Black patients carried 26 percent more active chronic conditions
than White patients with the same score, 4.8 against 3.8.

**The correction.** The authors did not stop at the finding. They
reformulated the prediction target so that it tracked illness rather than
cost, and reran the ranking. In the paper's own words, remedying the
disparity "would increase the percentage of Black patients receiving
additional help from 17.7 to 46.5%." One choice of prediction target, made
for defensible reasons, was suppressing eligibility for this population by
a factor of about two and a half.

![What the Obermeyer algorithm measured and what it was used for. Panel A: at
the score that triggers automatic enrollment, Black patients were
substantially sicker than White patients. Panel B: the share of enrolled
patients who were Black, as deployed and after the authors' correction.
Redrawn from the numbers reported in Obermeyer et al. 2019
[@pmid:31649194].](../images/obermeyer-cost-vs-illness.svg){#fig-obermeyer fig-alt="Two bar charts. Panel A shows active chronic conditions at the 97th risk percentile: 3.8 for White patients and 4.8 for Black patients. Panel B shows the share of automatically enrolled patients who are Black: 17.7 percent when ranked on predicted cost, 46.5 percent when ranked on illness."}

Now ask the bedside question. You are the primary care physician for one of
these patients. What would you have seen? Nothing. Your patient was not
enrolled in a program, and neither were most of your patients. The harm is
defined by a comparison across thousands of patients that no individual
clinician ever sees. What would have caught it was not a sharper instinct but
a denominator: someone auditing who was enrolled, by group, on purpose, with
the authority to act on what they found. That is the difference between this
case and the oximeter, and it is the reason both halves of the answer at the
end of this chapter are load-bearing.

### Two distinctions you will use all chapter

**Statistical bias versus social bias.** Statistical bias is a model's error
relative to the thing it was trained to predict. The Obermeyer algorithm had
very little of it; it predicted cost well. Social bias is a mismatch between
what was predicted and what should have been. A model can be statistically
excellent and socially disastrous at the same time, and the two objectives
are frequently in tension rather than merely different. When a vendor tells
you a model is accurate, you now know which of the two they are talking
about.

**Harms of allocation versus harms of representation.** The distinction is
Kate Crawford's, from a 2017 keynote at the NeurIPS conference. An
allocation harm is a resource distributed unfairly: a program slot, a
transplant listing, a dose of oxygen. A representation harm is a system
encoding a demeaning or erasing view of a group, whether or not any resource
changes hands: a model that reproduces a debunked claim about Black patients'
pain tolerance has harmed someone before a decision is made. Most of the
cases below are allocation harms. At least one is not, and the exercise asks
you to decide which.

### The catalog

::: {.callout-note title="A note on register"}
These cases are about harm to real patients along racial lines, and some
readers will have been on the receiving end of the systems described. The
chapter treats each one as an engineering post-mortem: a specific decision,
its consequence, and its correction. Whether the harm occurred is not in
question in any case here; it is documented. The work is in the mechanism.
:::

@tbl-proxies lists the cases this chapter draws on, in the four columns the
Do block will ask you to fill in for a case of your own. The fourth column is
the one to read slowly. "Identified" and "fixed" are different claims, and
the second needs its own verification.

| Case | What mattered, and what stood in for it | Who was harmed, through what decision | Correction, and status as of September 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pulse oximetry | Arterial oxygen saturation; light absorbance calibrated on light skin | Black, Hispanic, and Asian patients; oxygen and COVID-19 therapies delayed or never triggered [@pmid:33326721; @pmid:35639368] | FDA draft guidance, January 2025. **Still draft.** [@pmid:40042945] |
| Care management risk score | Health need; predicted health care cost | Black patients; excluded from care coordination at 2.6 times the corrected rate [@pmid:31649194] | Prediction target reformulated by the authors and, per the paper, by the vendor. Status of the industry's other scores: not known. |
| Kidney function (eGFR) | Measured filtration; creatinine with a race coefficient | Black patients; later CKD staging, later transplant referral [@pmid:32853499] | NKF-ASN Task Force recommended the race-free 2021 equation for all US laboratories [@pmid:34563581]. The widely quoted adoption figure [VERIFY: "roughly two-thirds of US labs" traces to a secondary source citing an unspecified survey]{.verify} could not be confirmed; a 2022 survey of 28 laboratories describes implementation but not national coverage [@pmid:38507611]. |
| Spirometry | Lung function relative to expected; expected value adjusted by race | Black patients; impairment normed away, with consequences for disability and transplant priority [@pmid:36383197] | ATS recommended race-neutral equations in April 2023 [@pmid:36973004]. **Actively contested.** Modeling across 249 million Americans estimates 12.5 million reclassified, with nonobstructive impairment rising 141% among Black and falling 69% among White persons, and disability payments shifting by over a billion dollars a year [@pmid:38767252]. Single-system transitions are being published as case studies [@pmid:40712949]. |
| Dermatology image AI | Disease across all skin tones; training images mostly of light skin | Patients with dark skin; missed or misclassified lesions [@pmid:35960806; @pmid:30073260] | Diverse benchmark datasets published; fine-tuning on them closed the gap in one study [@pmid:35960806]. No regulatory requirement for skin-tone reporting. |
| Chest radiograph AI | Radiographic disease; labels extracted from prior radiology reports | Female, Black, Hispanic, low-income, and uninsured patients, compounding at intersections; findings called normal [@pmid:34893776] | Documented; no correction adopted at scale. Who wrote the ground truth is the question. |
| Large language models | Physiology; text that reproduces race-based medicine | Black patients in particular; debunked claims about kidney function, lung capacity, and pain reproduced in clinical answers [@pmid:37864012; @pmid:38123252] | Vendor model updates, unversioned. Re-test with each release. |

: The proxy table. The Do block asks you to add a row. {#tbl-proxies}

Three things to notice across the rows rather than in any one of them.

**The proxies were all reasonable.** Cost is objective. Optical calibration
on available volunteers is how devices get built. Report text is the only
label available at radiograph scale. Race entered clinical equations through
observed population differences that someone was trying to account for. No
one in these cases set out to encode inequity, which is why "just don't be
biased" is not an available strategy and interrogating the prediction target
is.

**Correction is slower and messier than identification.** Obermeyer is
seven years old. The oximeter guidance is still draft. Race-neutral spirometry
is recommended and contested at once, and the contest is not a simple story:
the same equation change that lifts Black patients' disability eligibility
lowers White patients', and the 2024 modeling found the two equations
predicted respiratory outcomes about equally well, which means the choice
between them is not settled by accuracy [@pmid:38767252]. A student who
writes "we could not determine the adoption status" in the exercise has
answered correctly, and this chapter will say so again in the rubric.

**The bedside answers differ sharply by case, and that is the finding.**
Oximetry has a real bedside signal. Race-based equations were auditable by
anyone who read the equation, which was printed on the lab report the whole
time. The chest radiograph model and the care management score are close to
undetectable from a single encounter.

### The finding that complicates the bedside frame

It would be comfortable to leave this chapter believing that a careful
clinician catches these. The best evidence says otherwise.

In a randomized study, Jabbour and colleagues showed 457 hospitalist
physicians, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants a series of
vignettes of patients with acute respiratory failure, with chest radiographs,
and asked them to diagnose pneumonia, heart failure, or COPD
[@pmid:38112814]. Baseline accuracy was 73.0 percent. A standard AI model
raised it by 2.9 points, and by 4.4 points when the model also displayed an
explanation, a heat map showing where on the radiograph it was looking. A
*systematically biased* model, one built to be wrong in a consistent
direction, lowered accuracy by 11.3 points. Adding explanations to the biased
model recovered only 2.3 points, a difference that was not statistically
significant. Clinicians who could see the model's reasoning were not rescued
by it.

::: {.callout-important title="Necessary and insufficient"}
Individual vigilance catches the discrepancies that show up in the one
patient in front of you. The oximeter case is exactly that, and it is not a
small category. It does not catch harms that exist only in aggregate, and the
evidence says it does not reliably catch a confidently wrong model even with
the reasoning on screen. Institutional auditing by group and personal
skepticism are both load-bearing. Neither substitutes for the other.
:::

### Why this chapter does not teach you to fix the model

There is a literature of technical fixes: reweighting training data,
adversarial debiasing, post-processing thresholds by group. They are real,
and the fairness deck under Go deeper covers them. None of them would have
fixed the Obermeyer algorithm. The label was wrong, and no amount of
downstream adjustment fixes a wrong prediction target. That is a stronger
point than a survey of methods would have been, and it is why the question
this chapter hands you is about the target and not the math.

::: {.callout-note title="\"But it's FDA-cleared\""}
The oximeter was. So were the chest radiograph tools. Clearance answers a
different question from the one you are asking; the critical appraisal
chapter makes that case in full with the same 130 decision summaries cited
above [@pmid:33820998], and the FUTURE-AI table there gives fairness one row
and one question for the vendor. This chapter is that row, in depth. If the
two chapters are assigned in the same week, read the objection once and carry
it.
:::

## Watch or listen

**Podcast.** *NEJM AI Grand Rounds*, "The Double-Edged Sword of AI, with Dr.
Ziad Obermeyer" (27 July 2023; 74 min).
<https://ai-podcast.nejm.org/e/the-double-edged-sword-of-ai-with-dr-ziad-obermeyer/>

The first author of the cost-for-need paper, interviewed by two physicians
who build models. Listen for the phrase *task formulation*: his argument is
that the choice of what to predict, made before any data are touched,
determines more about bias than anything done afterward. That is the proxy
problem in the words of the person who documented it. Listen also for the
second half of his title: he describes work where an algorithm, pointed at
the right target, *reduced* a disparity that clinicians had been producing.
Twenty-five minutes covers the first argument; the rest is a good commute.
The episode is on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube if the NEJM player
does not load.

**If you would rather read.** The fairness deck at
<https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-05-ml-fairness/> is the seminar
this chapter was adapted from. It opens with two thought experiments, an
image search and a loan officer, that make the social-versus-statistical
distinction land without any medicine at all, and it carries the taxonomy of
bias sources you may want for Part B.

a classmate, or yourself. If you use a chatbot in the optional step, you are
asking it about a published paper, not about a person.

### Part A: the worksheet, on the case you already know (15 minutes)

This chapter walked the care management algorithm for you. Now do it on
paper, without looking back. Below is the artifact a clinician would actually
have seen: a tile in a population-health dashboard, drawn here to show what
was and was not visible.

Copy the worksheet into a document and fill in every line. The word
"utilization" on the tile is the only clue the clinician was given; decide
whether it was enough.

```
Case: Care management risk score (Obermeyer et al. 2019)

1. THE PROXY OR DATA GAP
   What quantity actually mattered, and what measurable thing was
   substituted for it?
   ____________________________________________________________________

2. WHO WAS HARMED
   Which population, and through what concrete decision? Name the decision
   that went differently, not just the group.
   ____________________________________________________________________

3. WHAT CORRECTION FOLLOWED
   ____________________________________________________________________

4. ADOPTION STATUS RIGHT NOW
   Finalized / adopted / partial / draft / contested / could not determine.
   Where does your answer come from?
   ____________________________________________________________________

5. THE BEDSIDE QUESTION  (spend the most time here)
   What could a clinician have caught WITHOUT knowing the algorithm's
   internals? What would you have seen, heard, or measured that did not
   fit? If your honest answer is "nothing," say so and say why.
   ____________________________________________________________________

6. Allocation harm, representation harm, or both? One sentence of defense.
   ____________________________________________________________________

7. Statistical bias, social bias, or both? One sentence.
   ____________________________________________________________________
```

Questions 1 through 4 are lookups. Question 5 is the exercise; if you wrote
a sentence there in under two minutes, go back.

### Part B: a case of your own (20 minutes)

Now add a row to @tbl-proxies for an algorithm in the specialty you are
entering. Two ways to find one.

**A search recipe.** In PubMed, run:

```
(algorithm OR "artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning" OR "risk score"
 OR "reference equation") AND <your specialty> AND (race OR "skin tone"
 OR "racial bias" OR disparities) AND (bias OR underdiagnosis OR "race-free"
 OR "race-neutral")
```

Filter to the last five years. Read three abstracts. Pick the one where you
can name, from the abstract alone, both what the tool was supposed to measure
and what it actually measured. If none of the three gives you both, that is
itself a finding; note it and pick the closest.

**Or a pre-vetted case.** Each of these is verified and carries at least one
open question about adoption, which is the part of the worksheet that teaches
the most:

- *Dermatology, primary care, oncology:* Daneshjou et al. 2022, the Diverse
  Dermatology Images benchmark [@pmid:35960806], with the 2018 viewpoint that
  predicted it [@pmid:30073260]. Note that the viewpoint is commentary, not
  data, and cite it as such.
- *Nephrology, internal medicine, transplant:* the race coefficient in eGFR,
  from the catalog of race-adjusted algorithms [@pmid:32853499] to the
  Task Force recommendation [@pmid:34563581].
- *Pulmonology, occupational medicine, surgery:* race-neutral spirometry,
  from the equation [@pmid:36383197] to the ATS statement [@pmid:36973004]
  to the modeling of what changes [@pmid:38767252]. This is the case whose
  correct question-4 answer is "contested"; do not flatten it.
- *Radiology, emergency medicine, critical care:* chest radiograph
  underdiagnosis [@pmid:34893776]. Ask specifically who wrote the ground
  truth.
- *Any specialty using a chatbot:* language models reproducing race-based
  medicine [@pmid:37864012] and encoding demographic stereotypes into
  differentials and plans [@pmid:38123252]. This is the case closest to what
  you will touch next year, and the one most likely to be a representation
  harm.

Fill in the same seven-question worksheet for your case. Then write your row
in the four columns of @tbl-proxies; that row is your artifact, and the paper
you found counts toward this week's resource log.

**Optional step, if you use a chatbot (5 minutes).** Ask your institutional
ChatGPT Edu or Copilot: *"What does `<the tool from your case>` predict, and
what is it used to decide?"* Then compare its answer to your worksheet line 1.
Does it name the proxy, or does it describe the tool as measuring the thing
it was hoped to measure? Models are good at the second and bad at the first,
because the papers they learned from mostly wrote it that way. If it named
the gap, note that it did; if it did not, you have just watched a proxy get
laundered into a fact, in real time, by a fluent source. Either result is
worth one sentence in your notes. If you do not use chatbots, skip this; the
exercise is complete without it.

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Worksheet line 1, both cases | Names the quantity that mattered *and* the thing measured, as two different things | Names the tool, or names one quantity |
| Worksheet line 2, both cases | Names the group and the decision that went differently for them | Names the group only |
| Line 4 | States a status and says where it came from; "could not determine" with a reason counts as meeting | A status with no source, or "fixed" without checking |
| Line 5, the care management case | Says "nothing at a single encounter" and names what would have been needed instead | Claims a bedside signal that does not exist |
| Line 5, your own case | Names a specific signal, or argues specifically why there is none | "Be careful" |
| Lines 6 and 7 | Each classification has a one-sentence defense, and you can say which cases are representation harms | Labels without defense |
| The one sentence | You can state the proxy problem without using the word "bias" | "Algorithms can be biased" |

## The standing question

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close this chapter. Two specifics.

First, go back to bed 14. The blood gas is back at 86 percent and the patient
is now on high-flow oxygen. Tomorrow on rounds, the attending asks why the
oximeter was wrong. Say what it measured and what you hoped it measured, in
one sentence, without the word "bias". Then say whether the patient should be
told, and what.

Second, you will use a clinical algorithm in your first month of residency
that nobody in this course has heard of. What is the one question you will
ask about it? Write your phrasing, not the chapter's. The live session
collects these in chat, and they are worth more than the table.

## Summary

- A proxy is a measurable stand-in for something that cannot be measured.
  Every canonical case of algorithmic harm in medicine is a proxy that
  tracked inequity: light for oxygen, cost for need, race for unmeasured
  exposure.
- The proxies were reasonable when chosen. That is why "don't be biased" is
  not a strategy and "what does this actually measure" is.
- Obermeyer: predict cost, get accuracy; use it for need, get a factor of
  2.6 in who was enrolled. Correction meant changing the target, not the
  model.
- Statistical bias is error against the target; social bias is the wrong
  target. Allocation harms move resources; representation harms need no
  decision at all.
- Identification is fast and correction is slow. The oximeter guidance is
  draft; race-neutral spirometry is recommended and contested.
- The bedside catches the oximeter and misses the risk score, and a biased
  model with explanations still lowered clinicians' accuracy by nine points.
  Vigilance and auditing are both load-bearing.
- The patient in bed 14 did not know the device was calibrated on people who
  did not look like him. Decide what you would tell him.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The anchor case in full, with the supplementary analysis of alternative
  labels [@pmid:31649194]. Twelve pages, and the clearest example in the
  literature of a correction that is a reformulation rather than a patch.
- The full catalog of race-adjusted algorithms, across cardiology,
  nephrology, obstetrics, urology, and pulmonology [@pmid:32853499]. Read it
  to see how many equations on your lab reports have a race term you never
  noticed.
- The spirometry contest as it stands: the ATS statement [@pmid:36973004]
  and the modeling of who is reclassified [@pmid:38767252]. Together they are
  the best available example of a correction whose costs and benefits land on
  different people.
- The oximeter regulatory story: the JAMA viewpoint on the draft guidance
  [@pmid:40042945] and the 34-device test against it [@pmid:40832401].
- Clinicians and biased models, with explanations [@pmid:38112814]. The
  supplementary material shows the heat maps the participants saw.
- Where the dermatology gap comes from and how it closes with data
  [@pmid:35960806].
- The language-model cases [@pmid:37864012; @pmid:38123252], and re-run
  their prompts on this year's model; the answers move.

**Talks**

- [Fairness in machine learning for healthcare](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-11-05-ml-fairness/),
  the deck this chapter was adapted from, including the mitigation methods
  this chapter deliberately left out and the reason they would not have fixed
  the anchor case.
- [AI and ML in an oncology service line](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-28-ai-ml-oncology-service-line/)
  for the institutional half of the answer: who audits, who monitors, and
  what "incorporate biography" means when race is standing in for exposure.
- Kate Crawford, "The Trouble with Bias", NeurIPS 2017 keynote, the source of
  the allocation-versus-representation distinction. On YouTube; about an
  hour. [VERIFY: stable URL and length before assigning]{.verify}
